Private Prayer
PRY-vit PRAIR
noun phrase
From Latin privatus (set apart, one's own) and precari (to entreat); private prayer is the secret converse of the soul with God, apart from the eyes of men.

Biblical Definition

Private prayer is the secret converse of the believing soul with God, offered apart from the eyes of men, in the closet of the heart and the chamber of the house. Our Lord taught it plainly: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly." Here is the very heart of the devotional life—not the prayer that performs for an audience, but the prayer that seeks the face of the Father alone. The closet door, shut against the world, shuts out also the hypocrite's temptation to be seen of men, that the soul may deal with God in simplicity and truth. Such prayer is the breath of the regenerate, the appointed means by which the saint casts every care upon God, confesses sin, pleads the promises, and holds communion with his heavenly Father through the one Mediator. Our Lord Himself, who needed no rebuke of hypocrisy, withdrew to solitary places and continued all night in prayer to God, leaving His people a pattern of secret devotion. The Father "which seeth in secret" observes the hidden groanings and the unspoken desires, and answers openly in His own time and way. The 1689 Confession names prayer, made "in the name of the Son, by the help of the Spirit, according to His will," as a part of natural worship due to God. Private prayer is the secret root from which all public godliness must grow.

Webster 1828 Definition

Secret prayer offered to God in solitude, apart from the observation of men; the personal and devotional communion of the soul with its heavenly Father.

PRAYER, n. From Latin precari, to entreat; with "private," secret devotion offered alone.

The act of addressing God in supplication, confession, and communion, performed in solitude and secrecy.

The personal and devotional intercourse of the believing soul with God, hidden from the eyes of men.

Our Lord's charge: "enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret" (Mat 6:6).

The secret root of godliness, observed and rewarded by the Father who seeth in secret.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:6 — "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly."

Luk 6:12 — "And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God."

Mar 1:35 — "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed."

Phi 4:6 — "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God."

Modern Corruption

No postmodern redefinition besets private prayer; its perennial enemies are the hypocrisy that prays to be seen and the busyness that crowds out the secret closet.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Private prayer is not the target of ideological revision; it is rather quietly abandoned. Its ancient enemy is the hypocrisy our Lord exposed—the prayer performed for the admiration of men—and its modern enemy is the crowded, distracted life that leaves no room for the shut door and the seeking of God in secret.

The principle to recover is that the closet, shut against the world, is the cradle of all true godliness. The Father who seeth in secret is the One the believer is to seek, casting every care upon Him through the one Mediator, by the help of the Spirit. The 1689 Confession names prayer a part of the worship due to God; our Lord's own withdrawal to solitary places is the saint's pattern. Public devotion can only be as deep as the secret prayer that feeds it.

Hebrew Roots

The phrase joins secrecy with prayer to name the hidden communion of the soul with God.

expand to see more

Greek tameion — inner chamber, storeroom, "closet"; the secret place of Matthew 6:6.

Greek proseuchomai — to pray; the verb of addressing God in worship.

Latin privatus — one's own, set apart; source of the English "private."

Latin precari — to entreat, beg; source of "prayer" and "precarious."

"The Father which seeth in secret" is the One to whom private prayer is addressed.

Usage

"Doctrinally, private prayer is a part of the natural worship due to God from every creature."

"Devotionally, it is the secret root and daily breath of the believer's communion with God."

"Pastorally, it guards against hypocrisy by seeking the Father's face rather than the praise of men."
